sources.text:
A question that sometimes arises is what should happen if a CPU tries to acquire a lock that the same CPU already holds. One line of reasoning is that this should be allowed: no other CPU can hold the lock, so there’s no need to worry about CPUs interfering with each others’ use of the protected data. Locking systems that allow a CPU to re-acquire a lock it already holds are called a re-entrant or recursive. On the other hand, if a lock is already held, even on the same CPU, that means an operation may have temporarily violated and not yet restored some invariants; to allow a new operation to commence while the invariants don’t hold seems like an invitation to bugs. Xv6 takes this latter view, and forbids a CPU that currently holds a lock from re-acquiring it. Detecting this situation is the purpose of the call to holding in acquire.

7.5 Locks and interrupts

Some xv6 spinlocks protect data that is used by both threads and interrupt handlers. For example, the clockintr timer interrupt handler might increment ticks at about the same time that a kernel thread reads ticks in sys_pause. The lock tickslock serializes the two accesses.

The interaction of spinlocks and interrupts raises a potential danger. Suppose sys_pause holds tickslock, and its CPU is interrupted by a timer interrupt. clockintr would try to acquire tickslock, see it was held, and wait for it to be released. In this situation, tickslock will never be released: only sys_pause can release it, but sys_pause will not continue running until clockintr returns. So the CPU will deadlock, and any code that needs either lock will also freeze.

To avoid this situation, if a spinlock is used by an interrupt handler, a CPU must never hold that lock with interrupts enabled. Xv6 is more conservative: when a CPU acquires any lock, xv6 always disables interrupts on that CPU. Interrupts may still occur on other CPUs, so an interrupt’s acquire can wait for a thread to release a spinlock; just not on the same CPU.

Most kernels, including xv6, interleave the execution of multiple activities. One source of interleaving is multiprocessor hardware: computers with multiple CPUs executing independently, such as xv6’s RISC-V. These multiple CPUs share physical RAM, and xv6 exploits the sharing to maintain kernel data structures that all CPUs read and write. This sharing raises the possibility of one CPU reading a data structure while another CPU is mid-way through updating it, or even multiple CPUs updating the same data simultaneously; without careful design such parallel access is likely to yield incorrect results or a broken data structure. Even on a uniprocessor, the kernel may switch the CPU among a number of threads, causing their execution to be interleaved. Finally, a device interrupt handler that modifies the same data as some interruptible code could damage the data if the interrupt occurs just as the interrupted code is also modifying the data. The word concurrency refers to situations in which multiple instruction streams are interleaved, due to multiprocessor parallelism, thread switching, or interrupts.

Xv6 has two types of locks: spinlocks and sleep-locks. We’ll start with spinlocks. Xv6 represents a spinlock as a struct spinlock. The important field in the structure is locked, a word that is zero when the lock is available and non-zero when it is held. Were there no concurrency, xv6 could acquire a lock with code like

Unfortunately, this implementation does not guarantee mutual exclusion in the face of concurrency. Two CPUs could simultaneously reach line 25, see that lk->locked is zero, and then both grab the lock by executing line 26. At this point, two different CPUs hold the lock, which violates the mutual exclusion property. What we need is a way to make lines 25 and 26 execute as an atomic (indivisible) step.

response.title: Spinlock Sharing Between Kernel Thread and Interrupt Handler: Deadlock and Disabling Interrupts
response.evidence_note: The supplied sources describe tickslock being shared by sys_pause and clockintr, the CPU-local deadlock scenario, the requirement that a CPU must not hold such a lock with interrupts enabled, and xv6's conservative rule of disabling interrupts on a CPU whenever it acquires any lock. Interrupts may still occur on other CPUs, so a remote acquire can wait for a thread to release a spinlock.

questions.stem:
In xv6, the spinlock tickslock protects ticks, which is incremented by the clockintr timer interrupt handler and read by a kernel thread executing sys_pause.

1. sys_pause holds tickslock while reading ticks.
2. The same CPU is then interrupted by a timer interrupt, so clockintr runs and tries to acquire tickslock.
3. clockintr sees that tickslock is already held and waits for it to be released.
4. On that same CPU, no interrupt occurs while interrupts are disabled, and xv6 disables interrupts on a CPU whenever it acquires any lock.
5. On other CPUs, interrupts and lock acquisitions may still occur.

Analyze this scenario and justify two design decisions: (a) why allowing a CPU to hold tickslock with interrupts enabled would deadlock this CPU, and (b) why, in the design used by xv6, acquiring any lock disables interrupts on that CPU but does not stop interrupts on other CPUs.

Give a short, step-by-step justification that refers to the actors, the lock state, and the local versus multiprocessor effects.
questions.answer:
(a) Deadlock on the same CPU:
- sys_pause holds tickslock and is running on the CPU with interrupts enabled.
- A timer interrupt arrives on that same CPU, so clockintr starts running there.
- clockintr tries to acquire tickslock, sees it is held, and waits for release.
- Only sys_pause can release tickslock, but sys_pause cannot resume until clockintr returns.
- clockintr cannot return while waiting for the lock, so the CPU is stuck: neither sys_pause can release the lock nor can clockintr make progress.
- Therefore, if a spinlock is used by an interrupt handler, a CPU must never hold that lock with interrupts enabled.

(b) Why xv6 disables interrupts on the acquiring CPU but allows other CPUs to receive interrupts:
- Disabling interrupts locally prevents the CPU that holds the lock from being interrupted by a handler that might try to acquire the same lock; this breaks the same-CPU cycle above.
- Interrupts on other CPUs do not create the same cycle because those CPUs do not hold the lock; if such a CPU's interrupt handler tries to acquire the lock, it can simply wait for the holder (the thread) to release it.
- Thus xv6's conservative rule of disabling interrupts whenever any lock is acquired on a CPU prevents local deadlock while still allowing interrupts elsewhere to wait on the lock.
- This matches the source: interrupts may still occur on other CPUs, so an interrupt's acquire can wait for a thread to release a spinlock; only on the same CPU is that impossible when the lock is held.
questions.explanation:
The key distinction is local versus remote interrupt behavior.
On the same CPU, if the interrupted code holds the lock and the interrupt handler needs that same lock, no progress can be made: the handler waits for the holder, and the holder waits for the handler to return.
Disabling interrupts on a CPU while it holds a lock removes that local cycle.
On other CPUs, the holder is not the interrupted code, so a competing acquire can wait normally until the lock is released.
The design therefore trades a small increase in interrupt latency for deadlock freedom.
questions.difficulty_reason: The learner must combine several constraints from the sources: the shared spinlock, same-CPU interrupt re-entry, the deadlock cycle, xv6's conservative rule for acquiring any lock, and the local versus multiprocessor distinction. The answer requires evaluating why the design works rather than restating a definition, and it must correctly distinguish same-CPU deadlock from remote waiting.

expected_steps: Identify that sys_pause holds tickslock and runs with interrupts enabled on the same CPU that will handle the timer interrupt.
Explain the same-CPU deadlock cycle: clockintr waits for tickslock, sys_pause cannot release because clockintr must return first.
State the rule that a spinlock used by an interrupt handler must not be held with interrupts enabled on that CPU.
Justify xv6's conservative design: acquiring any lock disables interrupts locally, avoiding same-CPU re-entry on any spinlock.
Distinguish local from remote effects: other CPUs may still take interrupts and wait for the lock without deadlocking the holder.

response.answer:
(a) Suppose sys_pause acquires tickslock but leaves interrupts enabled. While sys_pause is between acquiring and releasing tickslock, a timer interrupt fires on that same CPU. The CPU switches to clockintr, which tries to acquire tickslock. It finds that tickslock is already held, and because the holder is sys_pause on the same CPU, clockintr spins waiting for release. But sys_pause cannot run again to release the lock until clockintr returns; clockintr will not return until the lock is released. Thus the CPU is permanently stuck in a cycle: the interrupt handler waits for the interrupted thread, and the interrupted thread waits for the interrupt handler. No other CPU can break this cycle because only sys_pause holds and can release the lock.

(b) xv6 disables interrupts on the local CPU when any lock is acquired in order to prevent exactly this same-CPU interrupt/re-acquire deadlock. If a thread holds a lock and the same CPU takes an interrupt whose handler also needs that lock (or any lock that could be held by the interrupted code), the interrupt handler could spin forever waiting for the interrupted thread to release it. Disabling interrupts makes the lock acquisition and the protected critical section atomic with respect to interrupt handlers on that CPU. However, this does not stop interrupts on other CPUs. Those CPUs can still take timer or device interrupts and run handlers that acquire the same lock; they may spin until the local holder releases the lock, but that is safe because the local CPU can continue running and eventually release the lock. Disabling only local interrupts is therefore sufficient to avoid the self-deadlock while preserving responsiveness to devices on other CPUs.
